title: data sheet for ancient language datasets

content.text:
The template for **Data Sheets for Ancient Language Datasets** is based on the proposal by Gebru et al. 2021 (see https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.09010). The majority of questions is taken from there. However, as some questions are not relevant for historical data, they have been left out. On the other hand, questions which are of relevance for Humanities scholars researching ancient languages have been added. The question have been answered to the best of their knowledge by Daidalos Team. Sources for the information provided in the data sheet are listed in the bibliography section at the end of this document.

All links in this document have last been checked in Sept. 2025.

Perseus = Latin Dependency Treebank , UD Latin Perseus
PROIEL = Pragmatic Resources of Old Indo-European Languages, UD Latin PROIEL
SEFLAG = Systematic Evaluation Framework for natural language processing models and datasets in Latin and Ancient Greek
UD = Universal Dependencies
UDante = UDante Treebank, UD Latin UDante
CIRCSE = CIRCSE Treebank, UD Latin CIRCSE
LLCT = Late Latin Charter Treebank, UD Latin LLCT
ITTB = Index Thomisticus Treebank, UD Latin ITTB

content.section: Part I: Dataset Creation and Content

content.text: For what purpose was the dataset created? Was there a specific task in mind? Was there a specific gap that needed to be filled? Please provide a description.
content.answer:
The dataset consists the test splits of all latin treebanks part of version 2.15 of the Universal Dependencies Project (see below), namely: The dataset was created to serve as a goldstandard for the evaluation of classical language NLP tools as part of SEFLAG. The original goals of the UD treebanks (abridged from https://universaldependencies.org/introduction.html#introduction (as of Sept. 2025)): The Universal Dependencies (UD) treebanks were created to facilitate multilingual syntactic analysis and parsing by providing a standardized framework for dependency structures across languages. The goal was to support a broad range of tasks such as natural language understanding, machine translation, and cross-lingual studies, while addressing the lack of consistent linguistic annotations across diverse languages. 'The annotation scheme is based on an evolution of (universal) Stanford dependencies (de Marneffe et al., 2006, 2008, 2014), Google universal part-of-speech tags (Petrov et al., 2012), and the Interset interlingua for morphosyntactic tagsets (Zeman, 2008).' https://universaldependencies.org/introduction.html#introduction 
 CIRCSE: CIRCSE Research Centre in Milan 
 UDante:

content.text: What do the instances that comprise the dataset represent (e.g., documents, photos, people, countries)? Are there multiple types of instances (e.g., movies, users, and ratings; people and interactions between them; nodes and edges)? Please provide a description.
content.answer: The dataset consists of syntactically annotated sentences from a wide variety of languages. Each instance represents a sentence broken down into individual tokens (words or morphemes) with syntactic dependencies between them. The contents of the UD treebanks are themselves samples from the corpus of the surviving latin language material. See also section IV for more details on the content.

Tokens:

content.text: Does the dataset contain all possible instances or is it a sample (not necessarily random) of instances from a larger set? If the dataset is a sample, then what is the larger set? Is the sample representative of the larger set (e.g., geographic coverage)? If so, please describe how.
content.answer: The data used in the grc_ud_test_dataset_for_use_of_SEFLAG comprises the test splits of the Universal Dependencies Treebanks for Latin and thus represent a sample of the full data available at UD. Train and dev splits are also available at the UD website for each treebank (refer to the treebank hub pages linked above).

content.text: What data does each instance consist of? “Raw” data (e.g., unprocessed text or images) or features? In either case, please provide a description.
content.answer: Treebanks are stored as plain text files encoded with UTF-8 in the .conllu format (see: https://universaldependencies.org/format.html). Each file contains a number of sentences in tokenized form with linguistic annotations

content.text: Is there a label or target associated with each instance? If so, please provide a description.
content.answer: There are multiple labels associated with each instance conveying a range of linguistic as well as meta information for each sentence and each token inside a sentence. Refer to the UD guidelines and the treebank specific sites linked above.

content.text: Is any information missing from individual instances? If so, please provide a description, explaining why this information is missing (e.g., because it was unavailable). This does not include intentionally removed information, but might include, e.g., redacted text.
content.answer:
No information is missing from the instances, but not all annotations possible in the UD annotation scheme have been made (e.g. the treebanks usually do not contain Enhanced Dependencies). Additionally, not all fields existing in the UD annotation format have been filled for every token because not all tokens require every field.
All Treebanks follow slightly different interpretations of UD or are the result of automatic conversions, which do not result in 100% matching annotation styles between the treebanks. See also:     Federica Gamba and Daniel Zeman. 2023. Universalising Latin Universal Dependencies: a harmonisation of Latin treebanks in UD. In Proceedings of the Sixth Workshop on Universal Dependencies (UDW, GURT/SyntaxFest 2023), pages 7–16, Washington, D.C.. Association for Computational Linguistics.

content.text: Are relationships between individual instances made explicit (e.g., users’ movie ratings, social network links)? If so, please describe how these relationships are made explicit.
content.answer:
Each sentence is assigned an ID  which marks its position in the whole corpus
Each token inside a sentence is assigned a syntactic dependency relationship with it's head word.
